overview: The Justice Department moved to prosecute former FBI Director James Comey a third time, a week before midterm elections in which the final NPR/PBS News/Marist poll shows Democrats ahead by 8 points. Abroad, Lula won a fourth term in Brazil as his defeated rival Flávio Bolsonaro reportedly left for the US, and Israelis turned out in record numbers in an election seen as a verdict on Netanyahu. On Wall Street, Anthropic made its IPO filing public ahead of what could be the biggest stock debut ever, and the Fed is expected to hold rates on Wednesday. In New York, Gov. Hochul is making her pause on new data centers the centerpiece of her race's final week.

stories.headline: Justice Department moves to prosecute James Comey a third time
stories.summary: The Justice Department is trying for a third time to bring criminal charges against former FBI Director James Comey, this time alleging that he leaked classified national-defense information about a decade ago. Comey denies wrongdoing, and his lawyers say the case is legally invalid and was brought too late. Separately, a federal judge ruled that the department unlawfully fired his daughter, former federal prosecutor Maurene Comey.
stories.why_it_matters: Courts will now weigh whether a decade-old leak allegation can still be prosecuted, a test of how far the Justice Department can go in pursuing a longtime target of the president. Coverage came mostly from left-leaning and center outlets; only one right-leaning outlet in the ingest covered it.
stories.background: James Comey is a former FBI director and a longtime target of President Trump. The department's first case against him, brought in Virginia over his testimony to Congress, was dismissed by a judge, and he was later indicted in a separate case in North Carolina. In April, Bloomberg Government reported that prosecutors were also pursuing charges over alleged leaks of classified information. His lawyers say the newest case concerns a purported 2016 leak to The New York Times that was investigated years ago without charges.

facts.text: The Justice Department is seeking to prosecute Comey for a third time, alleging that he leaked classified national-defense information about 10 years ago.
According to unsealed court documents, prosecutors claim Comey directed the leak while he was leading the FBI.

Comey's lawyers say the case centers on a purported leak of national security information to The New York Times in October 2016, an issue they say was already investigated and did not lead to charges.
Comey denies wrongdoing, and his lawyers argue the case is legally invalid and falls outside the time limit for bringing charges.
CBS News reported that the department took steps to bring the charge earlier this month; NBC News reported that Comey has not been indicted in the latest case.

The New York Times reported that the department has stepped up moves against Comey and others as the midterms near, and that in some cases court paperwork shows signs of urgency, such as typos and the signatures of senior political leadership.
In April, Bloomberg Government reported that the department was pursuing additional charges against Comey over alleged leaks of classified information, after he had been indicted in North Carolina.
Separately, a federal judge ruled that the department unlawfully fired Maurene Comey, James Comey's daughter, from her job as a federal prosecutor in Manhattan and ordered her reinstated.
Maurene Comey was fired in July 2025 and had handled the prosecutions of Jeffrey Epstein and Sean Combs.

stories.headline: Justice Dept. asks Washington to hold 400 voters' ballots as court lets California count 20,000
stories.summary: The Justice Department asked Washington state to set aside ballots from more than 400 people it alleges are registered to vote without U.S. citizenship, a week before the midterm elections. A federal appeals court separately declined the administration's request to stop California from counting the ballots of about 20,000 voters the department has challenged on the same grounds. President Trump also offered a $1 million reward for voter fraud tips that lead to convictions.
stories.why_it_matters: With Election Day a week away, the moves bear on whether some voters' ballots are counted and on how far federal officials can reach into vote counting that states run. Most of the coverage came from left-leaning outlets.
stories.background: States, not the federal government, handle counting ballots and certifying results. The Trump administration has pressed claims that noncitizens are voting: in July the Justice Department warned Washington election officials that they could face criminal liability for keeping noncitizens on voter rolls, and this month it sued California and Los Angeles County to stop the counting of ballots from more than 20,000 people that federal agencies flagged as likely noncitizens. Officials in both states have pushed back: Washington's secretary of state accused the department of trying to intimidate election officials, and California's said it had not supplied evidence for its figure. Prosecuted cases of illegal voting by noncitizens remain rare, according to statistics cited by NewsNation.

facts.text: The Justice Department on Monday asked Washington state to set aside any ballots received from more than 400 people it alleges are registered to vote without U.S. citizenship.
Federal prosecutors said they sent a letter to Washington's secretary of state listing the 400 people.
The department said it had identified 1,500 votes cast by those more than 400 people in prior elections.

A federal appeals court declined the administration's request to block California from counting the ballots of 20,000 registered voters the department claims are noncitizens, so those ballots can be counted for now.
California Gov. Gavin Newsom accused Trump of an “assault on democracy.”

The department sued California and Los Angeles County this month to stop officials from counting ballots from more than 20,000 people that federal agencies flagged as “likely noncitizens” until their citizenship can be verified.
NBC News and The Guardian described the Washington request as the latest in a series of administration moves into ballot counting handled by states, including states with competitive midterm races.

In July, the department warned Washington election officials that they could be held criminally liable if they knowingly kept noncitizens on voter rolls; Washington's secretary of state called that letter part of “a troubling pattern of efforts to intimidate election officials.”
Trump offered a $1 million reward for voter fraud tips that lead to convictions; it was unclear where the money would come from.
Prosecuted cases of illegal voting or fraud by immigrants who do not have the right to vote remain rare, statistics show, NewsNation reported.

stories.headline: A week out, Trump campaigns in Mississippi and Texas as poll shows Democrats ahead
stories.summary: With one week until the midterm elections, President Trump campaigned Monday in Mississippi and Tuesday in Texas, where Republicans face competitive Senate races. The final NPR/PBS News/Marist poll before Election Day found Democrats with an 8-point lead among likely voters in the fight for Congress, though NPR flagged lagging enthusiasm among key groups.
stories.why_it_matters: The elections could shift control of Congress, which writes federal budgets and tax law and oversees the administration. Tens of millions of people have already voted.
stories.background: Midterm elections fall halfway through a president's term and can shift power in Washington and in statehouses. In deep-red Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom is challenging Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, and in Texas, Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton faces Democrat James Talarico in a competitive Senate race. Both contests have drawn late spending and visits from national figures. Polls have shown Republicans likely to do poorly, and Trump and the top Republicans in Congress have attacked such polls as fake.

facts.text: Trump campaigned Monday in Mississippi for Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, part of a closing rally blitz that the AP said highlights Republicans' challenges.

Democrats are making a play for the Mississippi seat, where Scott Colom is the Democratic challenger; the race has drawn millions in last-minute spending and high-profile visits, including a rally by Kamala Harris.
At the Mississippi rally, Trump responded at length to former President Barack Obama's criticism of his White House renovations, saying Obama “wouldn't understand.”
On Tuesday Trump was scheduled to rally in Corpus Christi and Lubbock, Texas, for Paxton, the Republican Senate nominee, who faces Democrat James Talarico.
Speaking to reporters before the trip, Trump said he would respect the midterm results “if they're honest.”
The chief justice of the Texas Supreme Court endorsed Talarico.
The New York Times reported that Paxton has taken about 350 trips outside Texas since he was sworn in as attorney general, which has drawn campaign scrutiny.

Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio planned to greet a newly arrived tanker carrying Venezuelan crude in Texas, which Bloomberg called a bid to showcase supply a week before the elections; Trump said Venezuela sent him 1 million barrels of oil as a “gift.”
The final NPR/PBS News/Marist poll before Election Day found Democrats with an 8-point lead among likely voters in the fight for control of Congress.
NPR said lagging enthusiasm among key groups is one sign that Democratic gains may not come easily.
In the same poll, 40% of people said their family finances had gotten worse.
Johnson and Thune, the top two Republicans in Congress, have joined Trump in calling polls “fake” as national surveys indicate the GOP is likely to do poorly.
Tens of millions of voters have already cast ballots.

“Midterm campaign blitz” presents Trump on offense, with no mention of Republican trouble.
A right-leaning outlet says early voting offers Republicans “little comfort,” pointing to an especially wide partisan gap.

stories.headline: Supreme Court leaves Texas-Justice Dept. deal limiting pauses in deportation cases in place
stories.summary: The Supreme Court on Tuesday declined to intervene against an agreement between the Trump administration and Texas that cuts off a way for immigration judges to pause some deportation cases. Opponents called the deal collusive and had asked the justices to restore a Biden-era rule that gave judges that discretion.
stories.why_it_matters: Immigrants with pending cases, such as crime victims or witnesses seeking other relief, lose a route to having deportation proceedings put on hold. Only left-leaning and center outlets in the ingest covered the ruling.
stories.background: A 2024 rule let immigration judges suspend some deportation cases, for example while a crime victim or witness sought other relief. In June, Texas sued to overturn it, the Justice Department agreed that the rule should be set aside, and U.S. District Judge Reed O'Connor entered a consent judgment vacating it. Baltimore, New Haven, Columbus and the group Centro Legal de la Raza tried to step in to defend the rule, but O'Connor ruled they lacked standing and the 5th Circuit declined to block the judgment, sending them to the Supreme Court.

facts.text: The Supreme Court on Tuesday left in force a settlement between the Trump administration and Texas that cuts off an avenue for pausing some deportations.
Immigrant advocates called the agreement “collusion” and had asked the justices to reinstate a Biden-era policy that gave immigration judges discretion.
The outcome means the administration can block immigration judges from closing or shelving deportation cases.
The 2024 rule let immigration judges pause some deportation cases, such as when a crime victim or witness is seeking relief.
After Texas sued in June, the Justice Department agreed that the rule should be set aside, and Judge Reed O'Connor entered a consent judgment vacating it.

O'Connor denied a request by Baltimore, New Haven, Columbus and Centro Legal de la Raza to join the case and defend the rule, finding they lacked standing, and the 5th Circuit declined to block the judgment.

An advisory from the Immigrant Legal Resource Center says immigration courts have read the decision broadly since June, using it to deny closures and terminations and to put already-closed cases back on the calendar.

stories.headline: Judge extends block on changes at D.C. public golf course Trump wants to overhaul
stories.summary: U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes extended an order barring the Trump administration from cutting more trees or making other changes at Washington's East Potomac Park without notice. Reyes noted that the president's social media posts contradicted sworn testimony from government officials. Trump said the administration would appeal and that the renovation would still start next month.
stories.why_it_matters: The fight is over public parkland near the National Mall, and the order means the government must give notice before it closes or alters the course. It also tests how a court responds when officials' sworn testimony conflicts with the president's public statements.
stories.background: East Potomac Golf Links is a century-old public golf course in East Potomac Park, near the National Mall, and Trump has sought to overhaul it. The DC Preservation League sued over the plans; in May, Reyes declined to issue a restraining order but told the National Park Service to consult government lawyers before cutting more than 10 trees. More than 500 trees have since been felled, and Reyes has now extended her block on further work.

facts.text: Reyes extended an order barring the government from clearing more trees or making other alterations at East Potomac Park without proper notice.
The order requires the government to give notice before closing or altering the property.
Reyes noted that the president's social media posts contradicted the sworn testimony of multiple government officials.
Reyes wrote that the court “does not speak for the trees” but “speaks only for the rule of law,” echoing an earlier line that she was “not the Lorax.”
More than 500 trees had been felled at East Potomac Golf Links before the halt, The Hindu reported.
Trump said the administration would appeal and that the renovation would still start next month; The Hindu put the planned start at Nov. 15.

The DC Preservation League brought the case; in May, Reyes declined to issue a temporary restraining order but told the National Park Service to discuss any plans to cut more than 10 trees with government lawyers first.

stories.background: Swalwell, a California Democrat, resigned from Congress amid a wave of sexual misconduct allegations, which he has denied. In August, according to a Reuters source, FBI agents seized his electronic devices at San Francisco International Airport and searched his home in Washington. Cloobeck, a wealthy developer, had been a Swalwell donor and associate.

stories.headline: Manhunt for convicted murderer who slipped through Tennessee prison fence
stories.summary: Authorities in several states are searching for Jacob Allen Morley, 28, who is serving a life sentence for murder and escaped from a state prison in Tiptonville, Tenn., by slipping through a perimeter fence. Officials say he stole a pickup truck after breaking out, and he remained at large on Tuesday.
stories.why_it_matters: Officials are asking residents to check home security cameras and watch for the stolen truck, and a friend of Morley's victim is warning the public that he is dangerous.

stories.headline: Lula wins a fourth term in Brazil as defeated rival Flávio Bolsonaro heads to the US
stories.summary: President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won Brazil's Sunday runoff against far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro after trailing him in the first round. Bolsonaro's party says it recognizes the result, but he has not conceded, and President Trump called the vote 'rigged' without offering evidence. Bolsonaro missed a deadline to hand his passports to police in a money-laundering inquiry, and sources cited by Reuters and other outlets say he has left for the United States.
stories.why_it_matters: Brazilians get four more years of Lula's government, but the loser's reported departure for the US and Trump's fraud claim set up friction with Washington. Markets fell sharply on the result, and a sinking currency can push up prices in Brazil while Lula decides how to pay for his campaign promises.
stories.background: Lula, the leftist incumbent, was seeking a fourth term against Flávio Bolsonaro, a senator and son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, who was a close ally of Donald Trump while in office. Flávio finished first in the first round earlier this month with about 47% of valid votes to Lula's 45%, according to the official count, which forced Sunday's runoff. The Trump administration has previously alleged that Jair Bolsonaro was a victim of judicial persecution in Brazil. Flávio is under federal police investigation over alleged corruption and money laundering, and a Supreme Court judge ordered him to surrender his passports hours after his loss.

Sources and media reports say he has left Brazil for the United States; the US embassy in Brazil did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Concern about how the economy will be managed gave Brazil's currency its worst day in more than 25 years, the Financial Times reported.
The result rattled Brazilian markets and leaves Lula weighing costly campaign promises against pressure to rein in spending, CNBC reported.

stories.headline: Israelis vote in record numbers in an election seen as a verdict on Netanyahu
stories.summary: Israelis voted Tuesday in the first national election since the Hamas-led attack of Oct. 7, 2023, a contest widely described as a referendum on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Turnout ran at its highest level in decades, and the Central Elections Committee turned down a request from the Likud and Shas parties to keep polls open longer. Polls close at 10 p.m. local time, and the result may not quickly settle who forms the next government.
stories.why_it_matters: The winner will lead Israel through unresolved wars in Gaza and with Iran, and NBC noted the outcome could affect the United States and gas prices.
stories.background: Netanyahu is already the longest-serving prime minister in Israel's history and is wanted by the International Criminal Court. His standing has been hurt by anger over the failure to prevent the Oct. 7 attack, wars in Gaza and with Iran, Israel's growing international isolation and the rising cost of living. He argues that only he can finish the job started in the war with Iran eight months ago, and President Trump has urged Israelis to return him to power. After the vote, parties must bargain to form a government, which is why the count alone may not decide who leads.

stories.headline: Local truce takes hold in Ukraine's Oleshky as Finland and Norway leaders call Putin
stories.summary: A local ceasefire brokered by US first lady Melania Trump took effect early Tuesday around the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in southern Ukraine, meant to let aid in and civilians out, while Russia fired missiles and drones at other Ukrainian cities. The same day, Finland's President Alexander Stubb and Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre held a rare direct call with Vladimir Putin about ending the war, drawing criticism from Denmark and Estonia.
stories.why_it_matters: The truce tests on a small scale whether Russia and Ukraine can hold a ceasefire, and the call shows Europe split over talking to Putin ahead of planned US-led peace talks that will shape the end of the war.
stories.background: Russia has occupied Oleshky, in the war-divided Kherson region, since February 2022, and residents have been cut off from food and medicine. On Oct. 23, Ukrainian, Russian and US negotiators agreed to pause fighting there so aid could enter and residents could leave through a safe corridor, and the White House credited Melania Trump with securing the deal. European leaders have mostly avoided direct contact with Putin, so the Finnish and Norwegian call broke with that stance. Stubb and Støre had held a joint press conference with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Oslo the week before.

facts.text: A local ceasefire around Oleshky took effect early Tuesday; Russia and Ukraine both said they would observe it from 3 a.m. local time.

Residents have been cut off from food and medicine, and the BBC reported that some ate weeds to survive.
Russia launched missiles and drones at cities across Ukraine, including Kyiv, as the truce began.
The front line near Oleshky was quiet for the first time in years, with both sides halting drone attacks, the Guardian reported.

Estonia's foreign minister, Margus Tsahkna, also expressed skepticism about the call in a post on X.
Kyiv said it hoped the call would bring 'new momentum' to peace talks.
Putin went on an extended tangent about Russian history during the call, the Financial Times reported.
The White House has proposed Russian deals for US oil majors as part of peace talks, in an effort to bring Putin to the table, the Financial Times reported.
Stubb, Støre and Zelenskyy held a joint press conference the week before, Norway's government said.

stories.headline: Congo's Ebola outbreak passes 10,000 confirmed cases
stories.summary: Confirmed cases in the Democratic Republic of Congo's Ebola outbreak rose above 10,000, government data showed Tuesday, and nearly half of those patients have died. The outbreak is driven by the Bundibugyo species of the virus, for which there is no approved vaccine or specific treatment, and cases have turned up in Kenya and Nigeria.
stories.why_it_matters: With no vaccine for this strain, containment depends on finding and isolating cases, and attacks on health workers and strikes over unpaid wages make that harder. Cases in Kenya and Nigeria show how far it can travel.
stories.background: The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, a rarer species of Ebola that the existing approved Ebola vaccine does not target. The World Health Organization declared the outbreak in Congo and Uganda a global health emergency in May. By early October Congo had reported more than 8,400 confirmed cases across seven provinces, including Ituri and North and South Kivu, according to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control. Cases have since been confirmed in Kenya and Nigeria.

stories.headline: Two men charged in UK over alleged Iran-backed plot at US-used air base
stories.summary: Two 24-year-old London men appeared in a London court Tuesday charged under Britain's National Security Act over a September incident at RAF Fairford, an English air base used by US bombers in the war against Iran. stories.why_it_matters: British authorities allege that Iran backed a plot against a base on British soil used by US forces in the war, a sign that the conflict's risks reach allies that host those forces.
stories.background: RAF Fairford is a base in England used by the US military, including bombers in its war against Iran. In September there was an incident at the base that British authorities have blamed on Iran. Counter-terrorism police arrested and later re-arrested suspects on suspicion of assisting Iranian intelligence, an offense under the National Security Act passed in 2023. On Tuesday prosecutors charged two men and they appeared in court in London.

facts.text: Mohmed Ahmad Abdulkarim, a British-Iranian dual national, and Nouman Essghir, a British citizen, both 24 and from London, were charged under the National Security Act.

stories.headline: Anthropic makes its IPO filing public, setting up what could be the largest stock debut ever
stories.summary: Anthropic, the company that makes the Claude chatbot, on Monday made public its paperwork to sell shares on the stock market, a step that several outlets say could lead to the biggest initial public offering in history. The filing says it plans to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker “ANT,” and MarketWatch reports it could pitch investors the week of Nov. 9 and begin trading as soon as the week after. The filing came on a day of very large AI fundraising deals, and European chip stocks rose on Tuesday on what The Wall Street Journal called renewed optimism about AI-linked stocks.
stories.why_it_matters: If the listing goes ahead, anyone with a brokerage account could buy shares in a major AI developer, and how investors receive it will show how much Wall Street is willing to pay for the AI boom.
stories.background: An initial public offering, or IPO, is when a private company first sells shares to the public on a stock exchange. Before it can do that, a U.S. company must file a document called an S-1, or prospectus, with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), laying out its finances, its plans and the risks it faces. Anthropic submitted a draft confidentially in June so regulators could review it privately; Monday's release made it public. The next step is a “roadshow,” in which the company and its banks pitch large investors before a share price is set. The listing comes as big tech companies spend and borrow enormous sums to build the data centers and chips that AI runs on. Disclosure: this brief is written by Claude, an AI model made by Anthropic, so read this story with that in mind and check the linked coverage.

facts.text: The Securities and Exchange Commission released Anthropic's S-1 filing on Monday, Oct. 26.
According to the filing, Anthropic plans to list on the Nasdaq exchange under the ticker “ANT.”

Anthropic first submitted the paperwork confidentially in June, which let the SEC review its finances before the public release; at the time it said the number of shares and the price had not been set.
Outlets including the Financial Times, NPR, the Associated Press, Axios and CNN said the offering could be among the biggest stock market debuts ever, and possibly the biggest.
With the filing public, Anthropic can hold its investor roadshow the week of Nov. 9 and would be eligible to start trading as soon as the following week, MarketWatch reported.

The prospectus includes warnings about AI itself: the BBC reported that Anthropic warned of “catastrophic risk” to humankind, the AP reported the CEO warned of risk to humanity, and the New York Post highlighted its description of chatbots' “self-preserving behaviors.”
A $63 billion debt deal for Anthropic, announced Monday, is the biggest ever to raise money for AI infrastructure, and Broadcom's CEO intervened to seal it, The Wall Street Journal reported.

Also on Monday, Meta announced plans to raise a total of $95 billion for AI infrastructure, with Nvidia and AMD set to invest $4 billion in Meta, and Meta and SpaceX both moved to raise billions more for AI.
Axios described a $235 billion AI dealmaking blitz led by the Anthropic filing, which it said nearly equals 1% of U.S. economic output (GDP).
European semiconductor stocks rose on Tuesday, which The Wall Street Journal tied to renewed optimism about AI-exposed stocks after the filing.
The New York Times reported that Wall Street banks and chipmakers are among those poised to benefit from the listing.

stories.headline: Fed is expected to hold rates this week, with more hikes possible later
stories.summary: The Federal Reserve's rate-setting committee meets Tuesday and Wednesday, and almost everyone surveyed expects it to leave its benchmark interest rate unchanged after raising it in September for the first time in three years. With inflation moving the wrong way and the job market steady, coverage says the focus is on whether Fed Chair Kevin Warsh signals more increases ahead.
stories.why_it_matters: The Fed's rate sets the tone for what you pay on credit cards, car loans and mortgages and what you earn on savings, so a signal of more hikes means borrowing could get more expensive. Only left-leaning outlets in today's feeds ran previews of the meeting.
stories.background: The Federal Reserve is the U.S. central bank. Its main tool is the federal funds rate, the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans, which ripples out to the rates people pay and earn. Raising it makes borrowing more expensive, which tends to cool spending and slow price increases; cutting it does the opposite. In September the Fed raised the rate by a quarter of a percentage point (25 “basis points”), to a range of 3.75% to 4%. The latest federal data show consumer prices up 3.7% in the year to September, well above the Fed's 2% goal, with unemployment at 4.2%.

The September increase was the Fed's first rate hike in three years, CBS News reported.
Kevin Warsh is in his first months as Fed chair.

Companies report results every three months, and investors often react as much to what a company says about the future, its “outlook,” as to the past quarter. stories.headline: Hochul runs on her data center pause in the governor's race's final week
stories.summary: A week before Election Day, Gov. Kathy Hochul is making the statewide pause on new data centers a centerpiece of her re-election campaign, Gothamist reports, after once resisting the idea. Her Republican opponent, Bruce Blakeman, says she failed to prepare for the industry. Separately, Hochul said her job would be "a lot easier" if Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu loses Israel's election, which is being held today.
stories.why_it_matters: New Yorkers choose a governor on Nov. 3, and early voting is open through Sunday. Both candidates pitch their data center stance as a way to hold down utility bills, and Blakeman has said he would rescind the pause, so the result decides whether it stays.
stories.background: Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul is seeking re-election against Republican Bruce Blakeman. In July she used an executive order to freeze new large data centers statewide for up to a year, the first such statewide pause in the country, after the Legislature passed its own moratorium bill that her office said needed more work. Hochul said the pause gives state agencies time to write rules so data centers pay their share of utility costs and protect the environment. Blakeman opposes a statewide moratorium and says local governments should be able to strike their own deals with tech companies. Siena's public polls have shown Hochul ahead by about 10 points since the summer.

facts.text: Gothamist reports that Hochul once resisted a pause on data centers but that the moratorium is now central to her campaign.
Blakeman says Hochul failed to prepare for the data center industry.
In July, Hochul moved by executive order to impose the country's first statewide moratorium on data centers, lasting up to a year.
Blakeman has criticized the moratorium, said local governments should be able to make data center deals, and said he would rescind the pause.
A Hochul campaign ad in September presented the moratorium as saving New Yorkers money on utility bills and attacked Blakeman for supporting new data centers.
A September Siena poll of likely voters had Hochul ahead of Blakeman by nine points, 50% to 41%, little changed from August.
Hochul said her job would be "a lot easier" if Netanyahu loses his election, blaming his policies for antisemitism locally, the New York Post and The Times of Israel reported.
Israelis are voting today on whether to oust Netanyahu after three years of war.
Early voting in New York runs from Oct. 24 through Nov. 1, and Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3.

stories.headline: No A trains between Rockaway Blvd and Lefferts Blvd for nine days starting Nov. 7
stories.summary: The MTA will suspend A train service between Rockaway Blvd and Ozone Park-Lefferts Blvd in Queens for nine straight days starting Nov. 7 while it replaces aging signals on the Liberty Avenue Line. Lefferts-bound trains will run to Howard Beach-JFK Airport instead, and free shuttle buses will cover the gap. The work is part of a larger signal upgrade on the A and C lines announced last week.
stories.why_it_matters: Riders on the Lefferts Blvd branch will need shuttle buses or other routes from Nov. 7 to Nov. 16. The broader project aims to replace old signals on the A and C lines in Brooklyn and Queens with a modern train-control system. Only amNY (center) covered the outage in today's ingest.
stories.background: The Liberty Avenue Line carries the A train's Lefferts Blvd branch through southern Queens. The MTA is replacing signals there and on the Fulton Street line in Brooklyn with communications-based train control. Gov. Kathy Hochul announced the start of the work on Oct. 22, calling it the largest subway signal replacement project in MTA history. The project is paid for with congestion pricing revenue.

stories.headline: City is slow to put agencies' records requests online, advocates say
stories.summary: The city has been slow to carry out a law requiring every agency to upload public records requests and data to an online portal, THE CITY reports, and good-government advocates say the delay holds back transparency. The City Council passed the bill last November.
stories.why_it_matters: The portal would let any New Yorker see what records people have requested from city agencies and what was released. Only THE CITY (center) covered this in today's ingest.
stories.background: New Yorkers can request records from city agencies under the state Freedom of Information Law, known as FOIL. Last November the City Council passed a bill, Intro 1235, sponsored by Council Member Gale Brewer, requiring city agencies to publicly report their FOIL requests through an online portal. Good-government groups testified to the Council in March and June about how the city is carrying out the law.

On Tuesday oil prices eased on diplomatic efforts in the Middle East and gold rose, while Boeing fell about 10% after slowing its 737 Max plans. concept.explanation: It's the interest rate banks charge each other for overnight loans, and it's the main lever the Federal Reserve pulls to steer the economy. The Fed sets a target range, now 3.75% to 4%, at meetings held eight times a year; this week's ends Wednesday. Raising it makes borrowing more expensive across the economy, which slows spending and, over time, cools inflation; cutting it does the opposite. You feel it fastest in credit card and savings account rates, which move within weeks. Mortgage rates follow longer-term Treasury yields instead, so they react to what investors expect the Fed to do over the next several years.
